cases.interviewerQuestion: What was it about mixing all three kinds of state into one store that actually produced the stale-state and re-render bugs — was there a specific bug that made the boundary between the layers obvious?
cases.tonyRaw: The core issue was that each layer has different consistency guarantees and lifecycles, and treating them as one store meant a component subscribing to that store re-rendered on every change regardless of which layer it actually cared about, plus you'd get server cache data and realtime presence data fighting over what was "current." The clearest case was around presence and cursor data living next to server-persisted document fields — a cache invalidation from TanStack Query would trigger re-renders on components that only cared about live cursor position, and conversely a Liveblocks presence update could momentarily clobber state that should have come from the server cache. Splitting them made the ownership of each piece of state explicit: Liveblocks owns the collaborative document and presence, TanStack Query owns anything server-persisted with its own invalidation rules, and local UI state stays in a reducer that neither of the other two touches. Once that boundary existed, the re-render scope for any given update became predictable instead of cascading through the whole tree.

cases.interviewerQuestion: You had to support two concurrent editor versions while integrating AI output into ProseMirror's typed node model — what made that dual-version constraint painful, and did it shape the design of the state-management layer itself?
cases.tonyRaw: The dual-version constraint was painful because ProseMirror's typed node model meant any schema assumption baked into the state-management layer for one editor version could silently break on the other — you couldn't just target the newer API and call it done, since millions of users were still on the old one in production. I co-led a team of 3 to 4 engineers on this and personally designed the state-management layer that integrated AI output into the document model, so I had to treat compatibility as a first-class constraint rather than an afterthought, which meant the layer couldn't assume a single shape for how AI-generated content mapped onto typed nodes. That shaped the design toward a more defensive, version-aware translation step between AI output and the document model, rather than a direct mapping, because the cost of getting it wrong was a broken editor for a real subset of users.

cases.interviewerQuestion: You mentioned tool-selection prompting improvements and artifact-type-picker logic as part of your contribution — what was actually going wrong with tool selection before that, and what made it hard to fix through prompting alone?

The issue was the model picking the wrong tool or artifact type when the input was ambiguous, which happened more often on longer or messier meeting transcripts where the signal for "what kind of output does this call for" was weaker. cases.interviewerQuestion: You mention validating calculation accuracy for high-volume trader accounts specifically — what made those accounts the hard case, and how did you actually confirm the ported numbers matched the old TypeORM implementation?
cases.tonyRaw: High-volume trader accounts are where the edge cases in trade metric computation actually surface — more fills, more open/close pairings, more of the aggregation logic getting exercised, so any subtle drift between the old and new implementation shows up there first instead of staying hidden. I worked on porting our trade metric computation from the TypeORM-based implementation into our new GraphQL API architecture, and rather than trusting the port by inspection, I validated calculation accuracy with stakeholders along the way, running the same accounts through both paths and comparing outputs. Where numbers diverged, that was the signal to go trace whether it was a rounding difference, an aggregation ordering issue, or an actual logic gap carried over from the old implementation. That stakeholder-in-the-loop comparison was really the only way to build confidence that the port preserved behavior rather than just preserving the code structure.

cases.interviewerQuestion: What was it about the delay and timing that kept pulling you back in for nine months — what specific failure mode were you chasing each time you adjusted it?
cases.tonyRaw: The core tension was always the same shape: too short a delay and you're firing saves on every keystroke, hammering the backend and creating noisy versions; too long and a user closes the tab or the app hiccups and you lose real work. I was chasing that failure mode specifically — data loss on the tail end versus save-spam on the front end — and the right delay wasn't a constant, it shifted as the artifact editor's usage patterns changed over those months. So it wasn't one fix, it was recalibrating the same tradeoff as I learned more about how people actually used the editor. I rotated off before the deeper stale-closure and grace-period work happened, which a teammate picked up afterward on the editor-specific hook.

cases.interviewerQuestion: By what percentage did your chunking strategy improve reliability on long meetings?
cases.tonyRaw: I don't have a percentage to give you, so I won't make one up. What I can say is what the design actually solved: instead of chunking everything up front, it tried the full transcript first and only split on actual context-window overflow, and when it did split, it broke at sentence or speaker boundaries instead of a fixed character cutoff. That mattered because a fixed cutoff can slice through the middle of a sentence or a speaker turn, which corrupts meaning right at the seam — boundary-aware splitting avoided that failure mode on long meetings specifically.

cases.interviewerQuestion: Before engineering you were an occupational therapist. Are you still licensed for that? I ask because I am curious whether the clinical background shaped how you approached the state architecture.
cases.tonyRaw: To answer directly: no, I'm not currently licensed, that was past-tense work before I moved into engineering. As for the connection, I'd be cautious drawing a straight line from OT to this architecture — the driver was really a concrete bug pattern, not a clinical mindset. We had one undifferentiated store handling real-time collaborative state, server-persisted state, and local UI state together, which caused stale-state and re-render bugs because those three things have completely different lifecycles. Splitting them into three layers — Liveblocks for the collaborative layer, TanStack Query for server state with proper cache invalidation, and a reducer for local UI state — was just matching the architecture to how the data actually behaved.

cases.interviewerQuestion: What tradeoffs came up during the data model design specifically — were there points where the shape you wanted for the GraphQL layer pulled against how the underlying data was structured?
